taxonomy.note: Modern accepted placement is Bouteloua dactyloides; many Texas sources still use the long-familiar synonym Buchloe dactyloides.

evidence: Hays — UT Austin Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve, N. Hays County explicitly records Buchloe dactyloides (accepted Bouteloua dactyloides).
Travis — Fowler (2002) documents Buchloe dactyloides as abundant in flat plots at Shield Ranch in western Travis County.

Williamson — UT Austin Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County includes the taxon under Buchloe dactyloides; BONAP county mapping independently supports the Texas county distribution.
target_zone_range.guardrail: BONAP county mapping used as the primary range authority; explicit county records used to name the three target counties. No county occurrence inferred from ecoregion alone.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at growth form and sex-specific inflorescences before anything else: buffalograss makes a creeping stoloniferous sod; male plants carry small flag-like spikes while female seed clusters are compact, bur-like, and tucked low among the leaves.
diagnostic_traits: perennial mat-forming shortgrass with stolons rooting at nodes
usually dioecious with strongly different male and female inflorescences
female inflorescences compact/bur-like and often partly concealed among leaves
male inflorescences with two or three short flag-like spikes
low dense turf/sod habit rather than a typical tall bunchgrass

confusers.separator: Blue grama is tufted to short-rhizomatous and normally shows 1–3 conspicuous curved eyebrow/rooster-comb racemes; buffalograss spreads as stoloniferous sod and has strongly dimorphic male versus female inflorescences.

Both can form low stoloniferous sod. Curlymesquite has conspicuously hairy/pilose stolon nodes and a different single zig-zag spike; buffalograss nodes are smooth and its female inflorescences are bur-like.
